items.requirement: The service must not manage its own user accounts or passwords and must instead authenticate staff using accounts issued outside the service by the platform company.

The service must isolate each drone operating company's data so that its fleet, jobs, sites, flights, and operational problems are visible only to that company's staff and cannot be viewed by other operating companies or by the platform's airspace desk.

The service must protect the personal data of staff in accordance with the GDPR, including minimizing exposure of personal identifiers across roles and tenants and supporting required data protection controls.
The service must allow a fleet technician to add new drones to their operating company's fleet and to retire existing drones so that retired drones can no longer be used for flights.

The service must allow a fleet technician to take a drone out of service for repairs and return it to service when repairs are complete, preventing drones that are out of service from being assigned to or signed off for a flight.
The service must allow a fleet technician to set up charging pads at their company's sites, maintain the working status of charging equipment, and send a drone to charge at an available charging pad.

The service must represent sites with their concurrent takeoff and landing capacity and must enforce that the number of drones taking off or landing at a site at the same time does not exceed that site's available places.

The service must allow the platform's airspace desk to maintain a shared airspace picture accessible to all operating companies, consisting of the network of flight corridors between sites and the zones that group those corridors.

The service must allow the platform's airspace desk to enter airspace closures announced by the authorities for prohibited zones, supporting both planned closures with a specified start and end time and sudden closures that take effect immediately.

The service must allow the platform's airspace desk to amend an existing airspace closure during the day, including widening the affected zones or changing the closure's end time, and immediately update the shared airspace picture.

When an airspace closure is entered or amended, the service must report to the airspace desk the aggregate disruption caused across customer companies without exposing any single operating company's fleet, jobs, sites, or specific operational problems.

The service must assist a dispatcher in identifying which of their company's available drones can reach the starting site of a job, taking into account drone availability, battery charge, and reachable flight corridors.
The service must never automatically select or assign a drone or a flight route for a job; a licensed dispatcher must explicitly choose both the drone and the flight corridor route for every flight.

The service must require a licensed dispatcher to explicitly sign off on a flight after choosing its drone and route before the flight is permitted to depart, and must record the dispatcher's sign-off for compliance with EU drone operation and EU U-space rules.
The service must prevent a flight from being signed off or departing if its chosen route passes through a zone with an active closure or a planned closure that overlaps the flight's window.
The service must allow a dispatcher to call off a flight of their operating company either before departure or while the flight is in progress.

When a sudden, planned, or amended airspace closure comes into force while drones from one or more operating companies are already in the air, the service must immediately identify all affected in-flight and scheduled drones and alert each affected operating company's dispatcher.

The service must ingest drone telemetry reports received through relay stations in a way that tolerates patchy radio coverage by deduplicating repeated reports, ordering out-of-order reports by event timestamp rather than arrival time, handling late reports without corrupting current drone state, and detecting missing reports when communication drops out.

The service must preserve the active flight state of a drone that restarts in flight after an onboard software fault and continues flying, associating subsequent telemetry reports with the ongoing flight rather than treating the restart as a new or terminated flight.

The service must monitor actual in-flight battery drain against remaining flight requirements—accounting for faster battery depletion in cold or windy conditions—and alert the responsible dispatcher when a drone's battery depletes faster than planned.

Because a single dispatcher may be responsible for hundreds of drones at once, the service must proactively surface exceptions and alerts—such as airspace closures affecting active flights, faster-than-planned battery drain, in-flight restarts, or lost radio contact—so the dispatcher does not have to manually watch every drone continuously.
